summary: This standards-track RFC updates CalDAV so clients and servers can exchange iCalendar data that refers to time zones by reference instead of including the full definition each time. It makes calendar data smaller. It updates RFC 4791.

plainLanguage.summary: Rather than copying the whole time zone rule book into every calendar event, you just point to the right page of it.

questions: how does caldav avoid sending vtimezone
subtitle: CalDAV clients and servers stop shipping bulky, unchanging time zone definitions with every calendar object.

tldr.problem: iCalendar requires every calendar object that uses a TZID to also carry the matching VTIMEZONE component, which can be larger than the event itself and is sent over and over.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises calendar-no-timezone and points to one or more time zone data distribution services. Clients then use the CalDAV-Timezones header with T or F, and new properties and elements that name a time zone by identifier.
tldr.outcome: Standard time zone definitions no longer need to travel with each exchange, which saves bandwidth, CPU and energy, especially on mobile or limited devices. The RFC updates RFC 4791.

today: RFC 7809 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016. It updates RFC 4791 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem With Bundled Time Zones
sections.content:
RFC 4791 (CalDAV) lets clients reach calendar data on a server in the iCalendar format. When an event uses local time, it names a time zone with a TZID parameter, and that name points to a VTIMEZONE component holding all the rules needed to work out UTC offsets.

iCalendar currently requires every VCALENDAR object that refers to a time zone by identifier to include the matching VTIMEZONE. These components are often larger, in octets, than the events or tasks that use them, and they rarely change. So large amounts of identical data are exchanged continuously, which hurts mobile or limited devices with little bandwidth, CPU and energy.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine stapling a thick book of clock rules to every birthday invite. The book almost never changes, so mailing it every time is a waste.

sections.title: The Idea: Time Zones by Reference
sections.content:
The IANA-hosted time zone database [RFC6557] provides the raw data for standard time zones, and a time zone data distribution service (RFC 7808) lets calendar applications fetch current definitions in a timely and accurate way. That service also gives CalDAV clients and servers a single reference on which to agree, so they no longer need to exchange the data for those definitions.

This RFC defines a new mode of operation in which iCalendar data is exchanged without VTIMEZONE components for known, standard time zones. It applies only to iCalendar data sent or received through CalDAV (RFC 4791, RFC 6638 and extensions). Other ways of exchanging calendar data, such as iTIP and iMIP, are not changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone agrees on one public library of time zone rules. Instead of passing the rules around, you just say which book to look up.

sections.title: What Servers Do
sections.content:
A server that supports this specification MUST include calendar-no-timezone in the DAV response header field of an OPTIONS response for a calendar home collection or calendar collection. It MUST also have one or more associated time zone distribution services and list them in the new CALDAV:timezone-service-set property on calendar home collections.

Servers MUST support the CalDAV-Timezones request header field. With the value T, the server MUST include all the VTIMEZONE components that are referenced. With F, it MUST NOT return VTIMEZONE components for identifiers provided by its advertised distribution servers, but it MUST still return the component for any time zone those servers do not offer. This applies to any HTTP request that returns iCalendar data, whether directly (a GET) or inside a response such as a DAV:multistatus.

If the header is absent, a server that advertises calendar-no-timezone MAY choose not to send standard VTIMEZONE components. The RFC notes that clients have typically ignored received time zone definitions in favor of their own built-in ones. Such servers need an administrator setting to override the default, for example based on the User-Agent value.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells clients which public library it uses. If a client says it already has the books, the server leaves them out, except for any odd zone that is not in the library.

sections.title: What Clients Do
sections.content:
Once a server advertises calendar-no-timezone, clients SHOULD send CalDAV-Timezones: F so that standard definitions are left out. They can send T to get every VTIMEZONE instead. With no header, clients can expect servers to leave out standard definitions and MUST get them from their own cache or from the distribution servers the CalDAV server advertises.

When sending data, clients SHOULD remove standard VTIMEZONE components whose identifier is available on one of the server's distribution servers. Clients MUST send definitions for any identifier those servers do not provide, and MUST be ready for the server to reject the data or map it to a standard zone.

Clients SHOULD also use the new CALDAV:calendar-timezone-id property and CALDAV:timezone-id element to set default and per-query time zones by identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks the server to skip the extra pages, and it only attaches a page of its own when it is using a zone nobody else has heard of.

sections.title: Unknown Zones and Identifier-Only Properties
sections.content:
A client may send a time zone that none of the server's services offer. The server then has three choices: keep the original definition so it can be returned to that client or others; refuse it, in which case it MUST reject the request with the CALDAV:valid-timezone precondition; or map it to an accurately matching standard zone and rewrite the iCalendar data to use the new identifier. Remapping is not appropriate for an attendee's copy of an event, because the organizer's client expects to see the original definition in iTIP replies.

The existing CALDAV:calendar-timezone property holds a full VTIMEZONE. The new CALDAV:calendar-timezone-id sets the default time zone by identifier. It MUST be present wherever CALDAV:calendar-timezone is supported, and its value MUST match the TZID inside that component. The server MUST accept either one and update the other. Setting the identifier to America/New_York, for instance, makes the server return the full data for that zone in the other property.

In the same way, calendar-query reports gain a CALDAV:timezone-id element as an alternative to CALDAV:timezone. If a client uses an identifier the server does not know, the server MUST reject it with CALDAV:valid-timezone, and the client MAY retry with the full component.
sections.plainLanguage: If you name a zone the library does not have, the server may keep your page, say no, or swap it for the closest real one. Naming a zone by its short name works the same way as handing over the whole page.

sections.title: New Properties, Elements and Header
sections.content:
CALDAV:timezone-service-set lists the URIs of the time zone data distribution servers as one or more DAV:href values. It SHOULD be defined on calendar home collections, and SHOULD NOT be returned by a PROPFIND DAV:allprop request.

CALDAV:calendar-timezone-id holds a time zone identifier as text. It SHOULD be defined on all resources that also define CALDAV:calendar-timezone, and likewise SHOULD NOT be returned by DAV:allprop.

The CALDAV:calendar-query element is modified so that its last part may be either timezone or timezone-id. Finally, the CalDAV-Timezones request header field is defined as T or F: T means the client wants time zone data returned, and F means it does not.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new labels are added to the calendar language: one for the library address, one for a zone's short name, and one switch that says yes or no to extra pages.

sections.title: Security, Privacy and IANA
sections.content:
Time zone distribution servers become a critical part of the calendaring architecture, which gives attackers a new target. Administrators of CalDAV servers SHOULD protect any advertised distribution servers to a level commensurate with the rest of the system. Otherwise the RFC adds no new security concerns beyond those of CalDAV, iCalendar and the time zone data distribution service.

For privacy, the recommendations in Section 9 of RFC 7808 SHOULD be used. An attacker could send a calendar user an event with a fake or rarely used time zone identifier and use lookups of it to monitor that user's activity, so those mitigations matter more.

IANA added the CalDAV-Timezones header field to the Permanent Message Header Field Registry, with protocol http and status standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Because everyone now looks things up in the shared library, it must be guarded well, and lookups should not reveal who is checking which page.

messages.label: OPTIONS
messages.note: Checks the DAV header for calendar-no-timezone.

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC ADDS TO CALDAV

items.label: calendar-no-timezone
items.desc: Capability token a server returns to OPTIONS on a calendar home or calendar collection.

items.label: CalDAV-Timezones
items.desc: Request header with value T (send VTIMEZONE) or F (leave standard ones out).

items.label: CALDAV:timezone-service-set
items.desc: Lists the time zone distribution servers; defined on calendar home collections.

items.label: CALDAV:calendar-timezone-id
items.desc: Default time zone of a calendar, set by identifier.

items.label: CALDAV:timezone-id
items.desc: Alternative to CALDAV:timezone in calendar-query reports.

items.label: CALDAV:valid-timezone
items.desc: Precondition used to reject an unknown time zone.
